Doros Dimosthenous sings Elvis - "Carnival with… the King"

The bass line starts walking, and suddenly you're somewhere else. Half Note transforms when rock and roll history enters — the jazz temple making room for hips that want to shake. Doros Dimosthenous takes the microphone, and Elvis Presley lives again in Athens. It's carnival season.

Elvis as jazz club material might surprise, but the connection runs deeper than novelty. Presley's early recordings drew from the same roots — blues, gospel, the spontaneous energy that defines improvised music. Dimosthenous understands this lineage. His interpretations don't just impersonate; they excavate, finding the musical intelligence beneath the cultural phenomenon.

Half Note during carnival season operates differently. The venue's usual solemnity softens, makes room for celebration that jazz purists might question but that the music itself endorses. The King's catalog — from "Heartbreak Hotel" through "Suspicious Minds" — contains multitudes that a jazz quartet can explore without betraying either tradition.

The crowd for carnival programming at Half Note mixes regulars with those drawn by the specific promise. You'll find people who've never entered the venue alongside those who hold season subscriptions, united by curiosity about what happens when Elvis meets Mets district, when rock iconography enters jazz territory.

The set will likely span the catalog's range — uptempo numbers that get even Half Note's reserved audience moving, ballads that reveal the songs' emotional architecture, deep cuts that reward the faithful. Dimosthenous and his band navigate between faithful tribute and jazz-informed reinterpretation, finding space for both.

If you need Elvis as historical artifact, if tribute to you means museum-piece recreation, this performance operates differently. The carnival context gives permission for joy that strict recreation wouldn't allow. But if you've been wondering what happens when a Greek vocalist applies jazz sensibility to the King's legacy, if carnival season means permission to dance at the temple — Half Note tonight answers the question.

Elvis at the jazz temple: carnival gives permission for what the music always wanted.

Doros Dimosthenous sings Elvis - "Carnival with… the King"

The blue spotlight hits the stage and suddenly you're in Memphis. The pompadour, the curled lip, the stance — but the voice that emerges carries something else, something that learned rock and roll through Greek speakers and Athenian nights.

Doros Dimosthenous has spent years channeling Elvis Presley, not as impersonation but as conversation. When a Greek singer inhabits the King's catalog, something strange and wonderful happens. The songs that defined American rebellion — "Suspicious Minds," "Can't Help Falling in Love," "Jailhouse Rock" — absorb Mediterranean inflection, the warmth of a culture that understood passion before rock and roll named it.

Half Note Jazz Club provides the setting this tribute deserves. Since 1979, this Mets institution has hosted jazz royalty, and tonight it bends its programming to honor a different kind of royalty. The room holds maybe 200 people, close enough to catch the performer's expression, intimate enough that Elvis's ballads fill the space without straining. The jazz club acoustic treats the voice as the instrument it is — every vibrato, every dramatic pause, every moment of surrender audible.

The crowd mixes unexpectedly. Elvis devotees who've seen every tribute share tables with Half Note regulars curious about the venue's departure from jazz. Greeks who grew up on rock and roll's international wave. Couples who fell in love to songs that Doros is about to deliver. The pre-show energy carries affection — people ready to be transported, permission already granted.

If you need pure authenticity, if only Elvis himself will do, tribute is always translation. Doros channels rather than copies, and the Greek angle adds rather than subtracts. But if you've been searching for an evening where the King's songbook meets Half Note's warmth, where rock and roll romance gets the intimate treatment it deserves — tonight, the blue suede shoes dance in Mets.

Elvis left the building decades ago. Tonight at Half Note, his songs find new rooms.

EDEN presents DARIA KOLOSOVA b2b HECTOR OAKS

The concert hall was built for classical music. Tonight it will discover what happens when Ukrainian techno precision meets Spanish-Berlin industrial weight, and neither artist has any interest in being polite about it.

Daria Kolosova has built her reputation on sets that refuse release. She accumulates intensity through layered percussion, hypnotic repetition, the relentless forward motion that defines Ukrainian techno's contribution to the European scene. Hector Oaks matches that intensity with different tools — his productions favor the hardware growl, sounds that feel machined rather than programmed. When they meet for back-to-back sets, the negotiation becomes the performance.

EDEN has secured the Athens Conservatoire for this encounter, and the setting sharpens everything. The venue has trained musicians since the 19th century; its halls carry the weight of tradition. Tonight that tradition absorbs frequencies its architects never anticipated, and the contrast makes the music hit differently. Dancing where classical musicians practiced scales — the irony operates on everyone present.

The crowd comes prepared for the collision. These are techno heads who track EDEN announcements, who recognize both names and understand what the B2B format promises. The Conservatoire's unfamiliar setting adds a layer — people genuinely curious whether the architecture can handle what's coming. (It can. The acoustics were built for sound, after all.)

If you need your techno in industrial spaces, if the venue should match the music's rawness, tonight inverts those expectations. The formality becomes fuel. But if you've been searching for the night that proves electronic music belongs in every room that's ever hosted serious music — the Conservatoire tonight learns new lessons from its students.

Daria Kolosova. Hector Oaks. The Conservatoire. Read those names again.

Doros Dimosthenous sings Elvis - "Carnival with… the King"

The sideburns catch the light before you hear the first note. Then the band kicks in and Memphis arrives in Mets, filtered through an Athenian voice that's spent years learning how the King made sound become feeling.

Doros Dimosthenous returns to Half Note for the second night of his Elvis tribute, and the word "tribute" barely covers it. This is inhabited performance — the gestures, the timing, the vocal catches that made Presley's catalog survive decades of imitation. Dimosthenous doesn't impersonate so much as channel, and the difference matters when the songs are ones you thought you knew completely.

Half Note Jazz Club offers the setting these ballads deserve. The Mets institution has hosted jazz royalty since 1979, and tonight it bends its programming toward rock and roll royalty of a different kind. The room holds maybe 200 people, close enough to catch the performer's expression, intimate enough that "Love Me Tender" actually feels tender rather than theatrical.

The Sunday night crowd differs subtly from Saturday's. Some are returners — people who came last night and couldn't stay away. Others are the ones who needed to hear how the first night went before committing. The result is a room even more prepared for what Dimosthenous delivers, permission for transport already granted before he takes the stage.

If you're a purist who believes no one should touch the King's catalog, if tribute feels inherently lesser, this evening asks you to reconsider. Dimosthenous proves that devotion can be creative, that interpretation honors rather than diminishes. But if you've been ready for an evening where Elvis's songs meet Half Note's acoustic intimacy, where the love songs land the way they're meant to — tonight, the King's spirit visits Mets again.

Same voice, same venue, different night. The songs remain immortal.

The Two Sides of the Atlantic Poetry and Colour in Music

The Stavros Xarhalambidis Quartet fills the Megaron's recital space with something rare in contemporary classical programming — a conversation between two continents that stopped pretending to be separate centuries ago. You're surrounded by SNFCC's polished modernism, but the sound tells a different story.

This isn't a lecture on "East meets West." It's four Greek musicians playing American standard bebop vocabulary over traditional Cretan harmonic structures, then inverting it. Xarhalambidis (piano) and Kostas Kouvakas (vibraphone) lead a rhythm section that understands both swing and the asymmetrical pulses of rebetiko. The program traces two centuries of cultural transmission — Portuguese traders bringing African rhythms to Greece, Greek immigrants bringing bouzouki sensibilities to Manhattan's 1920s, then modern players collapsing the distinction.

You'll find serious concert-goers: musicians familiar with Greek jazz traditions, classical patrons curious about the edges, tourists who stumbled in looking for opera. No one's checking their phone. People arrive early to read the program notes; they stay after to ask questions.

The Megaron's recital hall — 650 seats, intimate acoustic design — becomes less a concert space and more a room where careful listening happens. The musicians play close enough that you see the gesture before you hear the result. The arc of the evening moves from structured compositions (early sets) into exploration, where the quartet follows its own conversations and invites you to overhear.

If you need loud beats and crowds moving together, this is a concert hall, not a club.
